comments.author: @vladimirtchuiev2218
comments.text: The interesting thing is that there is a connection to Google's Titans memory module, where it uses the logits to express how "surprising" an idea is, and save it in a sort of a memory bank. This is the other direction, encouraging a model to output an "unsurprising" response, as the hypothesis is that the current answer is widely known. This can be an issue if you reach the long-tail data distribution where for a given query there is only a single answer in the data, no matter if it is right or wrong. The second issue is that it relies on statistical "certainty", where the majority answer is the encouraged one, and sometimes it's not the correct one.

They bring non-supervised learning to LLMs, that were based on self-supervised loss (use the same dataset for input and target); pretty big if you ask me. Would be interesting to check if unsupervised learning alone could be used for universe exploration, in a game like minecraft or asteroid, would it create new languages describing the world? I mean if you just need to be sure of your next token in a universe where you need control for reliably predicting the next step's possible/optimal actions :
1)if you die at a step the next actions could be pretty uniformly distributed because of the respawn randomness as compared to
2) continuing exploring where you could take the optimal actions not to die
 would this loss be enough?

I think this paper is also reminiscent of predictive coding (PC). Where each neural prediction needs to be predicted by other (often deepr) neurons. This is kind of the same thing at the level of answer text, where each seed used to randomly select token needs to interact the same way with the parameters, effectively predicting the same thing.

comments.author: @NathanielKeck
comments.text: Here's a weird take: when it gets down to the most acute level and I'm essentially using a model to serve my needs in agentic ways, I don't want a model that gives me the average base assumption of what the entire world's training data has taught it. Sure, when there's a fact based on empirical evidence and I am wrong about something to do with that fact, I'd like to be corrected and shown why I was wrong. But in matters of more nuance, maybe geared toward more sociological or personal matters, I don't want the biases of someone who isn't me or aligned with my world view to be influencing the model's outputs in a declarative way. This is one of the myriad reasons why AI must be given incentive to be inquisitive of those interfacing with them. Emotional intelligence is a subset of intelligence, but we don't hear about anyone working at the bleeding edge of that.
